cim_eredeti: Is AI the next dot-com bubble? ASU expert sees a key difference
szoveg_eredeti:
PHOENIX (AZFamily) — The wild swings on Wall Street have renewed fears that the artificial intelligence boom could end much like the dot-com bubble a quarter-century ago.

But Arizona State University finance professor Rawley Heimer sees fundamental differences between the two technological gold rushes. He is optimistic about the AI industry’s future, even as questions remain about soaring stock valuations.

“There’s real fundamental differences between what happened then and what’s happening now,” Heimer, a finance professor at ASU’s W.P. Carey School of Business, said on the latest episode of Generation AI.

Transformative technologies have historically fueled periods of intense financial speculation. From railroads to electricity to the internet, investors have lost fortunes betting on innovations even when the technology ultimately changed the world.

But unlike many of the companies at the heart of the dot-com bubble, Heimer said today’s leading AI companies are already generating substantial revenue and experiencing extraordinary growth.

“The financial weaknesses and in many cases, the complete lack of revenues for a lot of the companies that were at the heart of the dot-com bubble is not the same as what we’re experiencing today,” Heimer said.

Another reason for his optimism is the versatility of artificial intelligence. The technology has potential applications across numerous industries, and Heimer believes some of its most economically valuable uses may not have been discovered yet.

“I couldn’t be more bullish on it,” Heimer said of AI’s potential. “But at the same time, that’s different from having optimistic valuations about the companies that rely on AI.”

The challenge for investors is determining how long the AI industry’s extraordinary revenue growth can continue and whether stock prices accurately reflect companies’ future earnings, according to Heimer.

Those questions have taken on greater urgency following Anthropic’s record-setting initial public offering, a widespread stock market sell-off and a dramatic rally Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.

Heimer called Nvidia a “picks and shovels” company, supplying the essential tools for a technological gold rush. Demand for its chips can serve as an indicator of the health of the broader technology sector.

But Heimer cautioned that investors should consider how comfortable they are with so much of the stock market’s value being tied to a single company. The dramatic market reaction to Huang’s return also illustrates the financial risks of having so much riding on a single executive.

Another concern is the increasingly intertwined financial relationships among the companies building AI.

Critics have raised concerns about circular financing, in which chipmakers invest in AI developers that pay cloud computing providers, which in turn purchase more chips. The arrangement raises questions about how much demand is being fueled by investments within the industry itself.

Heimer acknowledged the potential risk but offered a counterargument: Technology companies may be better equipped than traditional financial institutions to identify promising AI investments because of their technical expertise.

“In some sense, we’re kind of trusting Nvidia to be a bank in a way,” he said.

Heimer is also less concerned about the enormous financial commitments AI developers are making to build out computing infrastructure. Anthropic disclosed in its IPO prospectus that it has committed to about $900 billion in future spending, almost entirely on computing power and infrastructure. Some of those agreements require payments even if demand falls short of expectations.

But Heimer said even if an individual AI company overestimates future demand, other businesses may be interested in using that computing power.

Ultimately, he said there is no single metric investors can use to determine whether the AI industry is in a bubble. One important measure, however, will be whether companies like Anthropic can turn rapidly growing revenues into profits.

For now, Heimer believes investors can be optimistic about the technology while skeptical of the valuations of AI companies.

“Those are two things that can exist at the same time,” he said.
